claims.text: Copper and nickel preferentially segregate to the surfaces of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Copper and nickel are lower-melting-point species within this alloy system.
Surface enrichment in lower-melting-point elements creates regions of reduced cohesive energy.
The reduced-cohesive-energy surface regions act as nucleation sites for premelting.
Surface segregation lowers and broadens the premelting-temperature regime relative to compositionally homogeneous nanoparticles.
The initial Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are chemically homogeneous and have a uniform BCC- or FCC-like solid-solution structure.
A mild pre-annealing treatment can induce controlled surface segregation in these nanoparticles.
Annealing produces a chemically heterogeneous surface layer that alters the local surface-bonding environment.
The segregated surface facilitates nucleation of a liquid-like layer below the bulk melting point of the homogeneous phase.
The high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles amplifies the segregation effect by reducing the effective barrier for a surface-initiated phase transition.
Segregation-inducing annealing will shift the onset of surface premelting downward by tens of kelvin relative to untreated homogeneous nanoparticles.
Segregation-inducing annealing will produce a broader and more gradual melting transition than in untreated homogeneous nanoparticles.
In situ TEM and DSC can reveal the predicted lower premelting temperature and broader melting transition.
The proposed behavior should apply primarily to nanoparticles smaller than approximately 20–30 nm, where surface effects dominate.
The behavior requires elemental melting-point and surface-energy differences large enough to drive segregation.
The magnitude of the temperature shift and transition broadening depends on nanoparticle size, stoichiometry, and segregation kinetics.
The comparison should use annealed and untreated batches with identical particle-size distributions.
A failure of confirmed surface-segregated particles to show both a greater-than-10-K premelting-onset decrease and transition broadening would falsify the hypothesis.
